query: For high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability to develop and retain a protective oxide layer that provides oxidation resistance? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison that would reveal it, the observations expected relative to a baseline, the applicable boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) develop and retain a protective oxide layer at high temperatures because dynamic processes (e.g., dynamic amorphization) create an ultra‐nanocrystalline near-surface region that is rich in high-angle grain boundaries. These boundaries serve as efficient nucleation and diffusion pathways for protective oxide formation, resulting in a more continuous and adherent oxide film compared to coarse-grained alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase, coarse-grained high-entropy alloy (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi) before exposure to high-temperature oxidative conditions.
generation.intervention: A controlled heat treatment or mechanical stress process designed to trigger dynamic amorphization and produce an ultra-nanocrystalline layer on the surface.
generation.conditions: High-temperature oxidation environments (e.g., 800–1000°C in air) that simulate operational conditions of high-temperature applications.
generation.structural_mediator: An ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer with a high density of grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The high density of grain boundaries in the nanocrystalline layer accelerates diffusion of oxygen and facilitates the rapid nucleation and growth of a coherent, protective oxide film. This layer ensures a more uniform and adherent oxide formation, reducing oxidation rates compared to alloys with a coarse-grained surface.
generation.predicted_outcome: HEAs pre-treated to develop the ultra-nanocrystalline surface will exhibit a more continuous, adherent, and slower-growing protective oxide layer during high-temperature oxidation, as evidenced by reduced mass gain and improved oxide layer morphology relative to untreated, coarse-grained HEAs.
generation.baseline: Untreated HEA samples that retain the coarse-grained microstructure and are exposed to the same high-temperature oxidizing conditions.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be significant in single-phase FCC high-entropy alloys similar to CoCrFeMnNi and at temperatures where diffusion kinetics are pronounced (e.g., 800–1000°C); effects outside these composition types or temperature ranges remain uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: The exact kinetics of oxide layer formation and the influence of different alloying elements on grain boundary chemistry and oxide adhesion are not fully established. Variations in the degree of nanocrystallization and its stability during prolonged high-temperature exposure may also affect outcomes.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples: one set undergoes a heat treatment or mechanical stress protocol designed to induce dynamic amorphization and form an ultra-nanocrystalline surface, while the control set remains in the coarse-grained state. Expose both sets to identical high-temperature oxidation conditions (e.g., 900°C in air) for a fixed period.
measurements: Surface and cross-sectional microstructural analysis (using SEM/TEM) to assess grain size and oxide layer continuity
Oxide layer thickness and adhesion (e.g., via nanoindentation or scratch testing)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-treated (ultra-nanocrystalline) samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in the uniformity, adherence, and reduced growth rate of the protective oxide layer compared to the coarse-grained control samples, then the hypothesis that the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline layer governs the superior oxidation resistance of HEAs would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties
